question: Why is Redis single-threaded, and how does it achieve >100,000 operations per second? Why is Redis single-threaded, and how does it achieve >100,000 operations per second?

options.text: It operates entirely in RAM and uses non-blocking I/O multiplexing (epoll/kqueue), eliminating thread context switches and lock contention.
It spawns one lightweight green thread per client connection internally, so it only appears single-threaded from the outside while actually using cooperative multitasking under the hood.
It shards its keyspace across 16 internal worker threads by hash slot, giving the appearance of a single thread to any one client while parallelizing across clients.
It relies on the operating system's kernel-level thread scheduler to interleave many blocking I/O calls so quickly that no explicit event loop is needed.

explanation: Specification answer: It operates entirely in RAM and uses non-blocking I/O multiplexing (epoll/kqueue), eliminating thread context switches and lock contention.

question: What is the difference between Redis RDB snapshots and AOF (Append-Only File) persistence? What is the difference between Redis RDB snapshots and AOF (Append-Only File) persistence?

options.text: RDB creates point-in-time binary disk snapshots; AOF logs every write command sequentially for near-zero RPO.
RDB logs every write command sequentially for near-zero RPO, while AOF creates periodic point-in-time binary snapshots, making AOF the faster option to restart from.
RDB and AOF are two names for the same persistence mechanism in modern Redis; the config option only changes the file extension used on disk.
RDB continuously streams changes to a replica in real time, while AOF is only used for one-time data export/import between different Redis instances.

explanation: Specification answer: RDB creates point-in-time binary disk snapshots; AOF logs every write command sequentially for near-zero RPO.

question: How does a Sliding-Window Rate Limiter work using Redis Sorted Sets? How does a Sliding-Window Rate Limiter work using Redis Sorted Sets?

options.text: Keys are timestamps; ZREMRANGEBYSCORE removes timestamps older than window; ZCARD checks count; ZADD appends current timestamp.
A single counter key is incremented with INCR on every request and reset to zero with EXPIRE at a fixed interval, without needing a sorted set at all.
Members are request IDs rather than timestamps; ZRANGEBYSCORE fetches all members, and the application counts how many fall inside the window in its own code.
ZADD stores the score as the request count rather than a timestamp, and the window is enforced by capping the sorted set's total size with ZREMRANGEBYRANK instead of by time.

explanation: Specification answer: Keys are timestamps; ZREMRANGEBYSCORE removes timestamps older than window; ZCARD checks count; ZADD appends current timestamp.

question: What is the difference between volatile-lru and allkeys-lru eviction policies? What is the difference between volatile-lru and allkeys-lru eviction policies?

options.text: volatile-lru evicts least recently used keys among those with an expire TTL; allkeys-lru evicts LRU keys across the entire database.
volatile-lru evicts keys across the entire database regardless of TTL, while allkeys-lru only evicts keys that have an expire set.
volatile-lru refuses to evict anything and instead returns an out-of-memory error to the client, while allkeys-lru is the only policy that actually removes keys.
Both policies only ever evict keys that have already expired; the difference is only in which background thread performs the deletion.

explanation: Specification answer: volatile-lru evicts least recently used keys among those with an expire TTL; allkeys-lru evicts LRU keys across the entire database.

question:
During triage in Redis Data Structures Persistence, an engineer observes:
"System fault during operation: Distributed Lock Race Condition Releases Another Worker's Lock".
What is the verified root cause?

options.text: Worker acquires lock with SET lockkey 1 EX 10. Worker takes 12 seconds to finish. Lock expires. Worker 2 acquires lock. Worker 1 then calls DEL lockkey, releasing Worker 2's lock prematurely.
Worker 1 sets the lock with SET lock_key 1 EX 10 but never checks the return value, so it proceeds to the critical section even when another worker already holds the lock, unrelated to expiry.
The lock key is stored with no expiration at all, so it never expires, and the race happens because two workers both call SETNX before either one's write is visible to the other.
Worker 2 acquires the lock using APPEND instead of SET, which merges its token with Worker 1's leftover value instead of replacing it, so both workers believe they hold a valid lock simultaneously.

explanation:
Root Cause: Worker acquires lock with SET lockkey 1 EX 10. Worker takes 12 seconds to finish. Lock expires. Worker 2 acquires lock. Worker 1 then calls DEL lockkey, releasing Worker 2's lock prematurely.

Fix Resolution:
Store a unique UUID token as the lock value and release exclusively via an atomic Lua script verifying token ownership before deleting.
